def: The list of folders the shell searches to find a program when you type its name. "command not found" means no folder in $PATH had it.
A file listing patterns Git should never track — build output, dependencies, and secrets like .env.
An absolute path starts at / and means the same thing everywhere; a relative path starts from your current folder.
A short-lived token sent to APIs, and a longer-lived, revocable token used to get new access tokens.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the four guarantees of database transactions.
Aggregates (count, sum, avg) summarise rows; GROUP BY summarises per group; HAVING filters the groups.
An allow-list describes exactly what's permitted and rejects the rest; a deny-list tries to name what's forbidden. Allow-lists are safer.
The set of requests a program accepts and the responses it promises — a contract other programs rely on.
A long-lived secret identifying a program or account; store only its hash, show it once, allow revocation.
The original 1960s code assigning numbers 0–127 to English letters, digits and symbols. The first 128 characters of UTF-8 are identical to it.
A queue guarantee that every message is delivered, but possibly more than once, so consumers must handle duplicates.
Authentication proves who you are (401 if it fails); authorization decides what you may do (403/404 if it fails).
OAuth's main flow: redirect to log in, get a one-time code, exchange it for tokens. PKCE stops stolen codes being used.
Automatically adding and removing copies of a service based on a signal such as CPU, requests per second or queue depth.
The programs that run on servers you control — storing data, enforcing rules, doing work the user's device can't be trusted with.
A backward-compatible change keeps existing clients working; a breaking change (rename, removal, new requirement) does not.
A way to write any bytes using only 64 safe text characters. Makes data about 33% bigger. Not encryption — anyone can decode it.
A single hardened server you SSH through to reach private machines.
Deliberately slow, salted password-hashing algorithms that make stolen hashes expensive to crack.
A token that grants access to whoever holds it, sent as Authorization: Bearer ….
Code that runs an operation many times and measures time and allocations per operation. In Go, BenchmarkXxx functions run with go test -bench.
A bit is a single 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits — a number from 0 to 255.
Broken object-level authorization: fetching objects by ID without checking the caller may access them. #1 API risk.
The scarcest resource in a system, which sets its capacity.
A named, movable label pointing at the latest commit of a line of work.
Isolating parts of a system (separate processes, pools or limits) so a problem in one can't exhaust resources the others need.
A fast copy of data kept closer (usually in memory) so you don't have to fetch it from somewhere slower. snip caches redirects in Redis.
A hit is found in the cache; a miss isn't. The hit ratio is hits ÷ all lookups.
Removing or updating a cached copy when the original changes.
Many requests missing the cache at once and all hitting the database for the same thing.
Check the cache; on a miss read the database and put the answer in the cache.
During a network partition, a distributed store must choose between consistency and availability.
Working out, from measured per-copy capacity and expected peak traffic, how many resources you need, with headroom.
Content delivery network: servers around the world that cache and serve static content close to users, so those requests never reach your servers.
A certificate binds a site's name to its public key; a CA is a trusted organisation that signs it.
Control group: a Linux kernel feature that limits and measures the memory, CPU, process count and I/O of a group of processes.
A typed pipe for passing values safely between goroutines.
chmod changes a file's permissions; chown changes its owner and group.
A wrapper around calls to a dependency that stops calling it after repeated failures (fails fast), then tests carefully for recovery.
The OAuth grant where a program authenticates as itself, with no user involved.
Teammates reading a change before it merges, to catch problems and share knowledge.
A database storing each column together, making scans and summaries over huge data very fast.
A snapshot of the whole project in Git, with a message, author, time and a link to the previous commit.
A compiler translates a whole program into machine code before it runs (Go); an interpreter reads and runs code line by line each time (Python).
An index on several columns, sorted by the first then the next — column order matters.
Concurrency is dealing with many things at once by switching between them; parallelism is doing several at the same instant on different CPU cores.
A small set of database connections opened once and shared by many requests.
A proxy like PgBouncer that accepts many client database connections and funnels them through a few real ones, protecting the database's connection limit.
A way of assigning keys to shards so that adding or removing a shard moves only a small fraction of the keys.
A rule in the schema — NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, foreign keys — that the database enforces on every write.
A set of workers sharing the messages of one stream or topic, with each message delivered to one member of the group.
A sealed box holding a program and everything it needs, run by a tool such as Docker.
A server that stores and serves images: Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, or a cloud provider's registry.
A response header telling browsers which scripts and resources may load — a strong XSS defence.
A value carrying a deadline and cancellation signal through all the functions working on one task.
A test that checks the code still matches its published contract.
A small value a server asks the browser to store and send back on every later request — how websites remember you despite HTTP being stateless.
A load-testing error where the load generator slows down along with the server, hiding the queueing and latency that real users would see.
Sharing data read-only until someone changes it, then copying just that piece. Containers use it so the image's layers never change.
Headers that let chosen other origins' browser scripts read your responses. Not a server-side access control.
Which lines of code your tests actually ran — a flashlight for untested code, not a score.
The processor: the part of a computer that follows instructions. Modern CPUs have several cores, each able to work independently.
A scheduler that runs commands at set times, described by five time fields.
Go's cryptographically secure random generator — use it for every key, token and salt, never math/rand.
Tricking a logged-in browser into sending requests the user never intended.
An organised collection of data, and the software (like PostgreSQL) that stores it safely and answers questions about it.
A holding area for messages that failed processing too many times, so they can be inspected rather than retried forever.
Goroutines or processes waiting on each other in a circle, so none can proceed.
Refusing access unless a rule explicitly allows it, so forgotten rules fail safe.
Someone else's code your project uses, pinned to a version.
Handing a component its dependencies from outside (e.g. passing a Store into a Service) so they can be swapped and faked.
Announcing that something will be removed, marking it, and giving clients time to move before removing it.
Proof, made with a private key and checked with the public key, that data came from the key holder and wasn't changed.
The internet's phone book: turns names like github.com into IP addresses.
Once a database confirms a write, it survives crashes and restarts.
Encoding changes format (anyone can reverse it); hashing is a one-way fingerprint; encryption hides data and needs a key to reverse.
A named piece of text a process carries (like SNIP_HTTP_ADDR=:8080) and passes to programs it starts, if exported.
Adding context to an error as it travels up (fmt.Errorf with %w) while keeping the original findable with errors.Is.
Copies may disagree briefly but converge once updates have spread.
The number a process returns when it ends: 0 for success, anything else for failure. It means the program didn't report an error — not that the result is right.
Changing a live schema safely: add the new thing, move data and code over, then remove the old thing later.
A Postgres command that runs a query and shows exactly how it was executed and how long each step took.
Stopping immediately with a clear error when something is wrong (like bad config), instead of limping on.
fetch downloads new commits without changing your files; pull fetches and merges; push uploads your commits.
Rules deciding which network traffic may reach a machine. Default: deny everything, allow only what's needed.
A test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails without any code change — a bug to fix, not ignore.
How computers usually store fractional numbers — fast but slightly imprecise (0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3). Never use it for money.
A column that must match a row in another table, keeping references valid; ON DELETE decides what happens when the parent goes.
Your own copy of someone else's repository on GitHub, used to propose changes back with a pull request.
The part of an app that runs on the user's device: the web page or mobile app.
A named, reusable set of steps that takes inputs (parameters) and can return outputs.
The shell expanding patterns like *.log into matching filenames before running a command.
A lightweight concurrent function in Go, started with the go keyword.
Stopping a server by refusing new work and letting in-flight requests finish before exiting.
A tool that keeps only the lines matching a pattern.
A contract-first way for services to call each other, with messages defined in .proto files and sent in a compact binary format.
A function that receives an HTTP request and writes the response; in Go, func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request).
The unique ID of a commit, calculated from its contents, like 4f3c9a1.
Turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint; the same input always gives the same hash, and it can't be reversed.
Git's "you are here": the branch (or commit) currently checked out.
Handling more load by running more copies of a service behind a load balancer. Requires the service to be stateless.
A single key (a viral link, a celebrity's profile) receiving a disproportionate share of traffic. Sharding doesn't help. Caching does.
The request–response language of the web. HTTPS is HTTP inside an encrypted TLS tunnel.
Cookie flags: hide the cookie from scripts, send it only over HTTPS, and don't send it on most cross-site requests.
A JWT from an identity provider stating who logged in (iss, sub, aud, exp).
The property that doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once, which makes retries safe. Often achieved with an idempotency key.
A unique ID a client sends with a request so a retry returns the original result instead of repeating the action.
An operation that has the same effect whether done once or many times. GET, PUT and DELETE are; POST is not.
A service that handles logins and issues tokens — Okta, Entra ID, Keycloak, Auth0 and others.
A read-only template for containers: a stack of filesystem layers plus settings (the command to run, user, ports). Built with docker build, shared through registries.
The SHA-256 hash of an image's contents (image@sha256:…). It always refers to exactly the same bytes.
One read-only slice of an image's filesystem, recording the files added or changed by one build step. Layers are shared between images and cached.
A movable, human-friendly label for an image version (postgres:16-alpine, latest). It can point to different images over time.
A sorted lookup structure that finds rows without scanning the whole table. B-trees are Postgres's default index.
A named list of methods describing what something can do. Any type with those methods satisfies it.
A machine's address on a network, like 203.0.113.10 (IPv4) or 2001:db8::10 (IPv6).
The standard way to write a date and time as text, e.g. 2026-09-24T19:56:18Z (the Z means UTC).
How much concurrent transactions can see of each other: Read Committed (Postgres default), Repeatable Read, Serializable.
Combining rows from two tables that match on a condition. An inner join keeps only matches; a left join keeps every row from the left table.
A table of pairs linking two other tables, such as link_tags between links and tags.
The command for reading logs collected by systemd's journal.
A command-line tool for querying and reshaping JSON.
A text format for structured data — objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. The language of most web APIs.
A JSON document of an issuer's public keys, used to verify its tokens' signatures.
A signed (not encrypted) token carrying claims like the user ID and expiry, verifiable without a lookup.
A private key you keep secret and a matching public key you share. Used by SSH, HTTPS and more.
SSH's record of each server's identity, checked on every connection to detect impostors.
How long you wait for something to respond. Memory, storage and networks differ in latency by factors of thousands.
Give every user and program only the access it needs, so a mistake or break-in can do limited damage.
In any stable system: items in the system = arrival rate × time each spends there (L = λW).
Liveness: is the process alive (restart if not)? Readiness: can it serve traffic right now (route around it if not)?
A component that spreads incoming requests across several copies of a service, skipping unhealthy ones.
Deliberately rejecting some requests when overloaded so the rest can still be served quickly.
Sending controlled, realistic traffic at a system to measure latency, throughput and errors as load changes. Variants: smoke, load, stress, spike, soak.
The name (address 127.0.0.1) that always means "this same machine".
Renaming, compressing and deleting old log files so they don't fill the disk.
Two transactions read the same value, change it, and write it back — one change disappears.
The computer's fast, temporary workspace. Everything in it is lost when the program stops or the power goes off.
Combining two lines of history. A conflict happens when both changed the same lines differently, and Git asks you to decide.
A buffer where one program leaves messages (jobs) and others pick them up later, decoupling the sender from the worker.
A function attached to a type, called with a dot: link.Describe().
Requiring two or more kinds of proof — something you know, have, or are.
Code that wraps every request handler to add shared behaviour: IDs, logging, metrics, authentication, panic recovery.
A numbered, version-controlled change to a database schema, applied in order exactly once everywhere.
Serving many customers (tenants) from shared infrastructure while keeping their data separate.
A lock that lets only one goroutine at a time into a section of code, protecting shared data.
Multi-version concurrency control: Postgres keeps row versions so readers and writers don't block each other.
Running one query for a list and then one more per item, instead of fetching everything in one or two queries.
A Linux kernel feature giving a process its own private view of one part of the system: process IDs, filesystem, network, hostname, users.
How a router lets many devices with private addresses share one public IP address.
Storing each fact in exactly one place, so updates can't leave conflicting copies.
SQL's marker for a missing or unknown value. Test it with IS NULL, never = NULL.
A standard for granting an app limited, revocable access to your data elsewhere without sharing your password.
Cheap, durable storage for files by key, like Amazon S3.
Open Container Initiative: the standards for container image formats and runtimes, so images work with Docker, containerd, Podman and Kubernetes alike.
OLTP systems handle live application reads and writes; OLAP systems scan large data for analytics.
The kernel mechanism that kills a process when memory runs out, or when a cgroup exceeds its memory limit. In Docker this shows as exit code 137 and OOMKilled.
An endpoint that redirects anywhere a parameter says — abused to make phishing links look trustworthy.
The standard machine-readable format for describing HTTP APIs: endpoints, requests, responses and errors.
A login standard built on OAuth: adds the signed ID token, discovery and published keys.
The program that manages the hardware and shares it between all other programs — macOS, Windows, Linux.
A widely used list of the most critical web application security risks, published by OWASP.
A package is one folder of Go code with one job; a module is a whole project with a go.mod listing its dependencies.
A tool (apt, dnf, brew) that installs, updates and removes software with its dependencies.
A small chunk of data travelling across a network with its destination address attached.
Returning a long list in pages. A cursor is an opaque marker meaning "continue after the last item you saw".
A phishing-resistant login using public-key cryptography stored on your device, replacing passwords.
A value that a given fraction of measurements fall below. p99 latency = 99% of requests were faster than this.
Read, write and execute rights for a file's owner, its group and everyone else, written like rw-r--r-- or 644.
The | operator: sends one program's output straight into the next program's input.
Sending SQL and its values separately ($1, $2) so values can never change the query — the cure for SQL injection.
The address of a value rather than a copy of it. A *T receiver lets a method change the original.
A number (1–65535) identifying one program on a machine, like an apartment number in a building.
Publishing a container's port on the host (docker run -p 9000:8080), since the container has its own network namespace.
A column (or columns) that uniquely identifies each row. Natural keys are real data like a slug; surrogate keys are invented IDs.
A running instance of a program, with its own private memory. The PID is its ID number.
A tool that samples what a program is doing (CPU, memory) to show where time or memory actually goes. Go's is pprof.
A branch (usually main) that can only change through reviewed pull requests with passing checks.
A proposed change from a branch, shown as a diff that others review, discuss and test before it's merged.
A bug where the result depends on the exact timing of two workers touching the same thing — for example two clicks counted as one.
Go's tool (go test -race) that reports unsafe concurrent access to memory while code runs.
Capping how many requests a client may make in a period, answering extra requests with 429 Too Many Requests.
Role-based access control grants permissions through roles; attribute-based access control decides from attributes and policies.
A copy of a database that continuously receives the primary's changes and serves read-only queries, adding read capacity.
A consistency guarantee that users always see their own writes, often achieved by reading from the primary right after writing.
Replaying your commits on top of another branch, rewriting them. Never rebase commits others already have.
An HTTP response (status 301, 302…) telling the client to go to a different URL, given in the Location header.
An in-memory data store used for caches, counters, rate limits and queues.
A mini-language for describing text patterns, such as ^ERROR or [0-9]+.
Another copy of the repository you exchange commits with, usually on GitHub. origin is the conventional name for the main one.
Keeping copies of a database on other machines; replicas follow the primary and serve reads.
How far a replica is behind the primary — why a just-saved change may not appear on a replica yet.
A unique ID given to each request, returned in a header and included in every log line, to connect reports with logs.
A thing an API deals with, named by a URL — a collection (/api/links) or an item (/api/links/godoc).
An API style where URLs name resources, HTTP methods are the verbs, and status codes report outcomes.
Trying a failed operation again after waiting, with the wait growing each time (often with random jitter), so retries don't pile onto a struggling service.
A server that sits in front of your application servers, receiving client requests and forwarding them (nginx, Caddy, a cloud load balancer).
Undoing a commit by adding a new commit that reverses it, leaving history intact.
root is the all-powerful administrator account. sudo runs a single command as root.
Matching a request's method and path (like GET /{slug}) to the handler that should answer it.
Locking rows you're about to change so concurrent transactions wait instead of conflicting.
Postgres policies that automatically restrict every query to the rows the current user or tenant may see.
A random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords get different hashes.
The shape of your data: tables, columns, types and the rules the data must obey.
A named permission requested by an app and recorded in its token, like links:read.
Any value that grants access or proves identity: passwords, keys, tokens, private keys.
A service that stores secrets encrypted, controls who may read them, audits access and supports rotation.
Replacing a secret with a new one, regularly and immediately after any suspected leak.
Automatically detecting secrets in code, commits, images or logs, often blocking pushes.
The core of reading data in SQL: which columns, which rows, in what order.
MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH version numbers: patch = fixes, minor = new features, major = breaking changes.
A named error value, like links.ErrNotFound, that callers can check for.
Reading every row of a table to answer a query — fine for small tables, slow for big ones.
A program that starts once, listens on a port and answers requests until stopped — and, by extension, the machine it runs on.
How a client finds the current addresses of a service's copies as they come and go, via DNS, a registry, or the platform (Kubernetes).
Server-side record of a logged-in user, referenced by a random ID stored in a cookie.
Bash's "strict mode": stop on errors, on unset variables, and on failures anywhere in a pipeline.
Splitting data across several independent databases by a shard key, so each handles part of the writes. Makes cross-shard queries and transactions hard.
The first line of a script, like #!/usr/bin/env bash, telling the OS which program runs it.
A file of shell commands that runs like a program — saved, repeatable typing.
A small message from the OS to a process. SIGTERM politely asks it to stop so it can clean up; SIGKILL stops it immediately.
Go's two everyday collections: a slice is an ordered list; a map looks values up by key.
A quick check that the basics of a system work end to end.
The link-shortener service you build throughout this handbook.
The one place whose data is authoritative; caches and copies are rebuilt from it.
Structured Query Language: the declarative language for querying and changing relational databases.
An attack where input glued into a SQL string changes the query itself.
Postgres's five-character error codes, e.g. 23505 for a unique violation.
Merging a pull request as a single commit, combining all of its commits.
An encrypted connection to a shell on another machine.
Carrying a connection through SSH so you can reach a private service, like a database, without exposing it.
Making a server fetch attacker-chosen URLs, often to reach internal systems.
Git's draft of the next commit: you choose which changes go in with git add.
Each request stands alone; the server doesn't depend on remembering the previous one. It's what lets any copy of a server answer any request.
A service where any copy can handle any request, because everything that must be remembered lives in shared storage, not inside one copy.
Types are known and checked by the compiler before the program runs, catching many mistakes early.
The three-digit number in an HTTP response: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
The three streams every program has: input, normal output, and error output.
A load-balancer setting that sends each user to the same backend copy. A patch for in-memory state, not a substitute for being stateless.
Where data is kept permanently. Much bigger and slower than memory.
A custom type grouping related fields, like snip's Link (Slug, URL, Clicks…).
Writing logs as named fields (usually JSON) so they can be searched and counted, rather than as free text.
Symmetric uses one shared key (AES); asymmetric uses a public/private key pair (RSA, Ed25519).
systemd starts and supervises services — programs that run in the background — restarting them when they crash.
A table holds one kind of thing; each row is one item; each column is one typed attribute.
A test that lists many input/expected-output cases in a table and checks them in one loop.
The slowest requests (p99, p99.9). It matters more as requests fan out to many services.
TCP delivers data reliably and in order over a connection (web, databases). UDP just sends packets with no guarantees (video calls, DNS).
A terminal is a text window; the shell is the program in it that runs your commands.
A simple stand-in for a real dependency, used to make tests fast and focused.
A worker inside a process. Threads share the process's memory.
How many requests (or jobs) a system completes per second.
A limit on how long to wait for something (a request, a query) before giving up and treating it as failed.
The encryption that turns HTTP into HTTPS: privacy, integrity and proof of the server's identity.
Decrypting HTTPS at the proxy or load balancer, which then forwards plain HTTP to the servers behind it on a private network.
A rate-limiting algorithm: a bucket of N tokens refills at a steady rate and each request takes one, allowing short bursts but enforcing an average rate.
A group of database statements that succeed or fail together (BEGIN … COMMIT / ROLLBACK).
How long something may be cached before it must be looked up again — used by DNS, caches and more.
A widely used checklist for services that run well on modern platforms: config in the environment, logs to stdout, and more.
Unit tests check small pieces fast; integration tests use real systems like a database; end-to-end tests exercise the whole running system.
Time as the number of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC.
A full web address: scheme, host, optional port, path, query and fragment.
The world's reference clock, with no time zone or daylight saving. Store times in UTC.
The standard way to store Unicode text as bytes; used by nearly the whole web.
The fraction of a resource's capacity in use. Waiting times rise sharply as it nears 100%.
Checking every input for size, syntax, meaning and business rules before acting on it.
A variable is a name for a value that can change; a constant never changes.
A system that records every change to a project over time, so you can go back, compare, and work in parallel. Git is the standard one.
Handling more load by giving one machine more resources (CPU, memory, faster disk). Simple, but limited, and one machine is a single point of failure.
Software that emulates a whole computer, running its own complete operating system, kernel included, on a hypervisor. Stronger isolation than a container, but heavier.
Storage mounted into a container from outside, so data survives when the container is removed.
A fixed number of goroutines (or processes) sharing a queue of jobs, keeping load bounded.
Giving a running program an identity so the platform issues it short-lived credentials — no stored secret.
Injecting script into pages other people view, so it runs in their browsers as the site.
What a Go variable holds before you set it: 0, "", false, or nil ("points at nothing").
